entries.96b4d27a45575c7e4cd6a47f0cabb751c326227f: <div sID="gen1148" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="36" osisID="Gen.36" sID="Gen.36"/> <div eID="gen1148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1149" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen1150" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have an account of the posterity of Esau, who, from him, were called Edomites, that Esau who sold his birthright, and lost his blessing, and was not loved of God as Jacob was. Here is a brief register kept of his family for some generations. 1. Because he was the son of Isaac, for whose sake this honour is put upon him. 2. Because the Edomites were neighbours to Israel, and their genealogy would be of use to give light to the following stories of what passed between them. 3. It is to show the performance of the promise to Abraham, that he should be "the father of many nations," and of that answer which Rebekah had from the oracle she consulted, "Two nations are in thy womb," and of the blessing of Isaac, "Thy dwelling shall be the fatness of the earth." We have here, I. Esau's wives, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.1-Gen.36.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. His remove to mount Seir, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.6-Gen.36.8">ver. 6-8</reference>. III. The names of his sons, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.9-Gen.36.14">ver. 9-14</reference>. IV. The dukes who descended of his sons, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.15-Gen.36.19">ver. 15-19</reference>. V. The dukes of the Horites, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.20-Gen.36.30">ver. 20-30</reference>. VI. The kings and dukes of Edom, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.31-Gen.36.43">ver. 31-43</reference>. Little more is recorded than their names, because the history of those that were out of the church (though perhaps it might have been serviceable in politics) would have been of little use in divinity. It is in the church that the memorable instances are found of special grace, and special providence; for that is the enclosure, the rest is common. This chapter is abridged, <reference osisRef="1Chr.1.35-1Chr.1.54">1 Chron. i. 35</reference>, &c.
entries.4f3539d631361f2d86ddb6995356a3fb4660a060: <div eID="gen1150" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen1149" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Generations of Esau. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1780.)</title> <div sID="gen1151" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the generations of Esau, who <hi type="italic">is</hi> Edom. <hi type="super">2</hi> Esau took his wives of the daughters of Canaan; Adah the daughter of Elon the Hittite, and Aholibamah the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon the Hivite; <hi type="super">3</hi> And Bashemath Ishmael's daughter, sister of Nebajoth. <hi type="super">4</hi> And Adah bare to Esau Eliphaz; and Bashemath bare Reuel; <hi type="super">5</hi> And Aholibamah bare Jeush, and Jaalam, and Korah: these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the sons of Esau, which were born unto him in the land of Canaan. 6 And Esau took his wives, and his sons, and his daughters, and all the persons of his house, and his cattle, and all his beasts, and all his substance, which he had got in the land of Canaan; and went into the country from the face of his brother Jacob. <hi type="super">7</hi> For their riches were more than that they might dwell together; and the land wherein they were strangers could not bear them because of their cattle. <hi type="super">8</hi> Thus dwelt Esau in mount Seir: Esau <hi type="italic">is</hi> Edom. <div eID="gen1151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1152" type="x-p"/> Observe here, 1. Concerning Esau himself, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.1">v. 1</reference>. He is called <hi type="italic">Edom</hi> (and again, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.8">v. 8</reference>), that name by which was perpetuated the remembrance of the foolish bargain he made, when he sold his birthright for <hi type="italic">that red, that red pottage.</hi> The very mention of that name is enough to intimate the reason why his family is turned off with such a short account. Note, If men do a wrong thing they must thank themselves, when it is, long afterwards, remembered against them to their reproach. 2. Concerning his wives, and the children they bore him in the land of Canaan. He had three wives, and, by them all, but five sons: many a one has more by one wife. God in his providence often disappoints those who take indirect courses to build up a family; yet here the promise prevailed, and Esau's family was built up. 3. Concerning his removal to mount Seir, which was the country God had given him for a possession, when he reserved Canaan for the seed of Jacob. God owns it, long afterwards: <hi type="italic">I gave to Esau mount Seir</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.5">Deut. ii. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.24.4">Josh. xxiv. 4</reference>), which was the reason why the Edomites must not be disturbed in their possession. Those that have not a right by promise, such as Jacob had, to Canaan, may have a very good title by providence to their estates, such as Esau had to mount Seir. Esau had begun to settle among his wives' relations, in Seir, before Jacob came from Padan-aram, <reference osisRef="Gen.32.3">ch. xxxii. 3</reference>. Isaac, it is likely, had sent him thither (as Abraham in his life-time had sent the sons of the concubines from Isaac his son into the east country, <reference osisRef="Gen.26.6">ch. xxv. 6</reference>), that Jacob might have the clearer way made for him to the possession of the promised land. During the life of Isaac, however, Esau had probably still some effects remaining in Canaan; but, after his death, he wholly withdrew to mount Seir, took with him what came to his share of his father's personal estate, and left Canaan to Jacob, not only because he had the promise of it, but because Esau perceived that if they should continue to thrive as they had begun there would not be room for both. <hi type="italic">Thus dwelt Esau in Mount Seir,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.36.8">v. 8</reference>. Note, Whatever opposition may be made, God's word will be accomplished, and even those that have opposed it will see themselves, some time or other, under a necessity of yielding to it, and acquiescing in it. Esau had struggled for Canaan, but now he tamely retires to mount Seir; for God's counsels shall certainly stand, concerning the times before appointed, and the bounds of our habitation.
entries.a1f5c4d05d30dc7d4b9d7e67e6996f83f682062a: <div eID="gen1152" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Dukes of Edom. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1729.)</title> <div sID="gen1153" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the generations of Esau the father of the Edomites in mount Seir: <hi type="super">10</hi> These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the names of Esau's sons; Eliphaz the son of Adah the wife of Esau, Reuel the son of Bashemath the wife of Esau. <hi type="super">11</hi> And the sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, and Gatam, and Kenaz. <hi type="super">12</hi> And Timna was concubine to Eliphaz Esau's son; and she bare to Eliphaz Amalek: these <hi type="italic">were</hi> the sons of Adah Esau's wife. <hi type="super">13</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the sons of Reuel; Nahath, and Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah: these were the sons of Bashemath Esau's wife. <hi type="super">14</hi> And these were the sons of Aholibamah, the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon, Esau's wife: and she bare to Esau Jeush, and Jaalam, and Korah. <hi type="super">15</hi> These <hi type="italic">were</hi> dukes of the sons of Esau: the sons of Eliphaz the firstborn <hi type="italic">son</hi> of Esau; duke Teman, duke Omar, duke Zepho, duke Kenaz, <hi type="super">16</hi> Duke Korah, duke Gatam, <hi type="italic">and</hi> duke Amalek: these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the dukes <hi type="italic">that came</hi> of Eliphaz in the land of Edom; these <hi type="italic">were</hi> the sons of Adah. <hi type="super">17</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the sons of Reuel Esau's son; duke Nahath, duke Zerah, duke Shammah, duke Mizzah: these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the dukes <hi type="italic">that came</hi> of Reuel in the land of Edom; these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the sons of Bashemath Esau's wife. <hi type="super">18</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the sons of Aholibamah Esau's wife; duke Jeush, duke Jaalam, duke Korah: these <hi type="italic">were</hi> the dukes <hi type="italic">that came</hi> of Aholibamah the daughter of Anah, Esau's wife. <hi type="super">19</hi> These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the sons of Esau, who <hi type="italic">is</hi> Edom, and these <hi type="italic">are</hi> their dukes. <div eID="gen1153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1154" type="x-p"/> Observe here, 1. That only the names of Esau's sons and grandsons are recorded, only their names, not their history; for it is the church that Moses preserves the records of, not the record of those that are without. Those elders that lived by faith alone obtained a good report. It is Sion that produces the men of renown, not Seir, <reference osisRef="Ps.87.5">Ps. lxxxvii. 5</reference>. Nor does the genealogy go any further than the third and fourth generation; the very names of all after are buried in oblivion. It is only the pedigree of the Israelites, who were to be the heirs of Canaan, and of whom were to come the promised seed, and the holy seed, that is drawn out to any length, as far as there was occasion for it, even of all the tribes till Canaan was divided among them, and of the royal line till Christ came. 2. That these sons and grandsons of Esau are called <hi type="italic">dukes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.36.15-Gen.36.19">v. 15-19</reference>. Probably they were military commanders, dukes, or captains, that had soldiers under them; for Esau and his family lived <hi type="italic">by the sword,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.27.40">ch. xxvii. 40</reference>. Note, Titles of honour have been more ancient out of the church than in it. Esau's sons were dukes when Jacob's sons were but plain shepherds, <reference osisRef="Gen.47.3">ch. xlvii. 3</reference>. This is not a reason why such titles should not be used among Christians; but it is a reason why men should not overvalue themselves, or others, for the sake of them. There is an honour that comes from God, and a name in his house that is infinitely more valuable. Edomites may be dukes with men, but Israelites indeed are made to our God kings and priests. 3. We may suppose those dukes had numerous families of children and servants that were their dukedoms. God promised to multiply Jacob, and to enrich him; yet Esau increases, and is enriched first. Note, It is no new thing for the men of this world to be full of children, and to have their bellies too <hi type="italic">filled with hidden treasures,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Ps. xvii. 14</reference>. God's promise to Jacob began to work late, but the effect of it remained longer, and it had its complete accomplishment in the spiritual Israel.
entries.3019ba4990f5ca92f7cb98d6ed56858bf54b3bcb: <div eID="gen1154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1155" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the sons of Seir the Horite, who inhabited the land; Lotan, and Shobal, and Zibeon, and Anah, 21 And Dishon, and Ezer, and Dishan: these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the dukes of the Horites, the children of Seir in the land of Edom. 22 And the children of Lotan were Hori and Hemam; and Lotan's sister <hi type="italic">was</hi> Timna. <hi type="super">23</hi> And the children of Shobal <hi type="italic">were</hi> these; Alvan, and Manahath, and Ebal, Shepho, and Onam. <hi type="super">24</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the children of Zibeon; both Ajah, and Anah: this <hi type="italic">was that</hi> Anah that found the mules in the wilderness, as he fed the asses of Zibeon his father. <hi type="super">25</hi> And the children of Anah <hi type="italic">were</hi> these; Dishon, and Aholibamah the daughter of Anah. <hi type="super">26</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the children of Dishon; Hemdan, and Eshban, and Ithran, and Cheran. 27 The children of Ezer <hi type="italic">are</hi> these; Bilhan, and Zaavan, and Akan. <hi type="super">28</hi> The children of Dishan <hi type="italic">are</hi> these; Uz, and Aran. <hi type="super">29</hi> These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the dukes <hi type="italic">that came</hi> of the Horites; duke Lotan, duke Shobal, duke Zibeon, duke Anah, <hi type="super">30</hi> Duke Dishon, duke Ezer, duke Dishan: these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the dukes <hi type="italic">that came</hi> of Hori, among their dukes in the land of Seir. <div eID="gen1155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1156" type="x-p"/> In the midst of this genealogy of the Edomites here is inserted the genealogy of the Horites, those Canaanites, or Hittites (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.26.34">ch. xxvi. 34</reference>), that were the natives of Mount Seir. Mention is made of them, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.6">ch. xiv. 6</reference>, and of their interest in Mount Seir, before the Edomites took possession of it, <reference osisRef="Deut.2.12">Deut. ii. 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.2.22">22</reference>. This comes in here, not only to give light to the story, but to be a standing reflection upon the Edomites for intermarrying with them, by which, it is probable, they learned their way, and corrupted themselves. Esau having sold his birthright, and lost his blessing, and entered into alliance with the Hittites, his posterity and the sons of Seir are here reckoned together. Note, Those that treacherously desert God's church are justly numbered with those that were never in it; apostate Edomites stand on the same ground with accursed Horites. Particular notice is taken of one Anah who fed the asses of Zibeon his father (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.24">v. 24</reference>), and yet is called <hi type="italic">duke Anah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.36.29">v. 29</reference>. Note, Those that expect to rise high should begin low. An honourable descent should not keep men from an honest employment, nor a mean employment hinder any man's preferment. This Anah was not only industrious in his business, but ingenious too, and successful; for he found <hi type="italic">mules,</hi> or (as some read it) <hi type="italic">waters, hot-baths,</hi> in the wilderness. Those that are diligent in their business sometimes find more advantages than they expected.
entries.6ee96d647449b5381d3047d714f80783da8b71fe: <div eID="gen1156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1157" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the kings that reigned in the land of Edom, before there reigned any king over the children of Israel. <hi type="super">32</hi> And Bela the son of Beor reigned in Edom: and the name of his city <hi type="italic">was</hi> Dinhabah. <hi type="super">33</hi> And Bela died, and Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his stead. <hi type="super">34</hi> And Jobab died, and Husham of the land of Temani reigned in his stead. <hi type="super">35</hi> And Husham died, and Hadad the son of Bedad, who smote Midian in the field of Moab, reigned in his stead: and the name of his city <hi type="italic">was</hi> Avith. <hi type="super">36</hi> And Hadad died, and Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his stead. <hi type="super">37</hi> And Samlah died, and Saul of Rehoboth <hi type="italic">by</hi> the river reigned in his stead. <hi type="super">38</hi> And Saul died, and Baal-hanan the son of Achbor reigned in his stead. <hi type="super">39</hi> And Baal-hanan the son of Achbor died, and Hadar reigned in his stead: and the name of his city <hi type="italic">was</hi> Pau; and his wife's name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred, the daughter of Mezahab. <hi type="super">40</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the names of the dukes <hi type="italic">that came</hi> of Esau, according to their families, after their places, by their names; duke Timnah, duke Alvah, duke Jetheth, <hi type="super">41</hi> Duke Aholibamah, duke Elah, duke Pinon, <hi type="super">42</hi> Duke Kenaz, duke Teman, duke Mibzar, <hi type="super">43</hi> Duke Magdiel, duke Iram: these <hi type="italic">be</hi> the dukes of Edom, according to their habitations in the land of their possession: he <hi type="italic">is</hi> Esau the father of the Edomites. <div eID="gen1157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1158" type="x-p"/> By degrees, it seems, the Edomites wormed out the Horites, obtained full possession of the country, and had a government of their own. 1. They were ruled by kings, who governed the whole country, and seem to have come to the throne by election, and not by lineal descent; so bishop Patrick observes. These kings reigned in <hi type="italic">Edom before there reigned any king over the children of Israel,</hi> that is, before Moses's time, for <hi type="italic">he was king in Jeshurun,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.33.5">Deut. xxxiii. 5</reference>. God had lately promised <hi type="italic">Jacob that kings should come out of his loins</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.11">ch. xxxv. 11</reference>), yet Esau's blood becomes royal long before any of Jacob's did. Note, In external prosperity and honour, the children of the covenant are often cast behind, and those that are out of covenant get the start. The triumphing of the wicked may be quick, but it is short; soon ripe, and as soon rotten: but the products of the promise, though they are slow, are sure and lasting; <hi type="italic">at the end it shall speak, and not lie.</hi> We may suppose it was a great trial to the faith of God's Israel to hear of the pomp and power of the kings of Edom, while they were bond-slaves in Egypt; but those that look for great things from God must be content to wait for them; God's time is the best time. 2. They were afterwards governed by dukes, again here named, who, I suppose, ruled all at the same time in several places in the country. Either they set up this form of government in conformity to the Horites, who had used it (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.29">v. 29</reference>), or God's providence reduced them to it, as some conjecture, to correct them for their unkindness to Israel, in refusing them a passage though their country, <reference osisRef="Num.20.18">Num. xx. 18</reference>. Note, When power is abused, it is just with God to weaken it, by turning it into divers channels. <hi type="italic">For the transgression of a land, many are the princes thereof.</hi> Sin brought Edom from kings to dukes, from crowns to coronets. We read of the dukes of Edom (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.15">Exod. xv: 15</reference>), yet, long afterwards, of their kings again. 3. Mount Seir is called <hi type="italic">the land of their possession,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.36.43">v. 43</reference>. While the Israelites dwelt in the house of bondage, and their Canaan was only the land of promise, the Edomites dwelt in their own habitations, and Seir was in their possession. Note, The children of this world have their all in hand, and nothing in hope (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.25">Luke xvi. 25</reference>); while the children of God have their all in hope, and next to nothing in hand. But, all things considered, it is better to have Canaan in promise than mount Seir in possession.  <chapter eID="Gen.36"/> <div eID="gen1158" type="x-p"/>

entries.8f5bb7b2b4b1076030af3fad8d503fbdf8a01bde: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv410"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 36</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gen.36.1-Gen.36.43">Ge 36:1-43</reference>. Posterity of Esau.</title> <div sID="gen604" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv410"/><hi type="bold">1. these are the generations--</hi>history of the leading men and events (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.2.4">Ge 2:4</reference>).<div eID="gen604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen605" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Esau who is Edom--</hi>A name applied to him in reference to the peculiar color of his skin at birth [Ge 25:25], rendered more significant by his inordinate craving for the red pottage [Ge 25:30], and also by the fierce sanguinary character of his descendants (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.12">Eze 25:12</reference>; Ob 10). <div eID="gen605" type="x-p"/>
entries.4c394e18f83c681e1cc5de1c8705a02389d84e02: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv411"/><div sID="gen606" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv411"/><hi type="bold">2-3. Esau took his wives of the daughters of Canaan--</hi>There were three, mentioned under different names; for it is evident that Bashemath is the same as Mahalath (<reference osisRef="Gen.28.9">Ge 28:9</reference>), since they both stand in the relation of daughter to Ishmael and sister to Nebajoth; and hence it may be inferred that Adah is the same as Judith, Aholibamah as Bathsemath (<reference osisRef="Gen.26.34">Ge 26:34</reference>). It was not unusual for women, in that early age, to have two names, as Sarai was also Iscah [Ge 11:29]; and this is the more probable in the case of Esau's wives, who of course would have to take new names when they went from Canaan to settle in mount Seir. <div eID="gen606" type="x-p"/>
entries.2dc9f60bf61417b19bac8b824d69307b3dfad5bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv412"/><div sID="gen607" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv412"/><hi type="bold">6-7. Esau ... went into the country from the face of his brother Jacob--</hi>literally, "a country," without any certain prospect of a settlement. The design of this historical sketch of Esau and his family is to show how the promise (<reference osisRef="Gen.27.39">Ge 27:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.27.40">40</reference>) was fulfilled. In temporal prosperity he far exceeds his brother; and it is remarkable that, in the overruling providence of God, the vast increase of his worldly substance was the occasion of his leaving Canaan and thus making way for the return of Jacob. <div eID="gen607" type="x-p"/>
entries.d5067a4999a2a13b8fb80f28de722874180be1e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv413"/><div sID="gen608" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv413"/><hi type="bold">8. Thus dwelt Esau in mount Seir--</hi>This was divinely assigned as his possession (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.4">Jos 24:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.2.5">De 2:5</reference>). <div eID="gen608" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a3d43b178b3276481cdecff551ff0187e0db38a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv414"/><div sID="gen609" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv414"/><hi type="bold">15-19. dukes--</hi>The Edomites, like the Israelites, were divided into tribes, which took their names from his sons. The head of each tribe was called by a term which in our version is rendered "duke"--not of the high rank and wealth of a British peer, but like the sheiks or emirs of the modern East, or the chieftains of highland clans. Fourteen are mentioned who flourished contemporaneously. <div eID="gen609" type="x-p"/>
entries.0962084b4df09cfc60768902d565c588859582cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv415"/><div sID="gen610" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv415"/><hi type="bold">20-30. Sons of Seir, the Horite--</hi>native dukes, who were incorporated with those of the Edomite race. <div eID="gen610" type="x-p"/>
entries.01f4c7d4f22133f302437eed0fc8a2ad372fe0e5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv417"/><div sID="gen612" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv417"/><hi type="bold">31-39. kings of Edom--</hi>The royal power was not built on the ruins of the dukedoms, but existed at the same time. <div eID="gen612" type="x-p"/>
entries.933e3070f6ff7ffb98c50e93a41d15ba282c0cd9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv418"/><div sID="gen613" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv418"/>40-43. Recapitulation of the dukes according to their residences. <chapter eID="Gen.36"/>

entries.aa5ad00a964d5e72ea56b0c89deecb6c99684fd1: <div eID="gen1714" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen1715" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen1716" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen1716" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen1715" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen1717" type="x-p"/> The genealogy of Esau, i.e., his sons, by his Canaanitish wives Adah, Aholibamah, and Bashemath, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.1-Gen.36.3">Gen 36:1-3</reference>. The children of Adah and Bashemath, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.4">Gen 36:4</reference>. Of Aholibamah, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.5">Gen 36:5</reference>. Esau departs from Canaan and goes to Mount Seir, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.6-Gen.36.8">Gen 36:6-8</reference>. The generations of Esau, i.e., his grandchildren, while in Seir, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.7-Gen.36.19">Gen 36:7-19</reference>. Anah finds mules (Yemim) in the wilderness, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.24">Gen 36:24</reference>. The generations of Seir, the Horite, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.29-Gen.36.30">Gen 36:29-30</reference>. The kings which reigned in Edom, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.31-Gen.36.39">Gen 36:31-39</reference>. The dukes that succeeded them, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.40-Gen.36.43">Gen 36:40-43</reference>. <div eID="gen1717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1718" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen1718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1719" type="x-p"/> These are the generations of Esau - We have here the genealogy of Esau in his sons and grandsons, and also the genealogy of Seir the Horite. The genealogy of the sons of Esau, born in Canaan, is related <reference osisRef="Gen.36.1-Gen.36.8">Gen 36:1-8</reference>; those of his grandchildren born in Seir, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.9-Gen.36.19">Gen 36:9-19</reference>; those of Seir the Horite, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.20-Gen.36.30">Gen 36:20-30</reference>. The generations of Esau are particularly marked, to show how exactly God fulfilled the promises he made to him, Genesis 25 and 27; and those of Seir the Horite are added, because his family became in some measure blended with that of Esau.
entries.1fb585e61876ef55233b83eaf9f138d900135c32: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen1719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1720" type="x-p"/> His wives - It appears that Esau's wives went by very different names. Aholibamah is named Judith, <reference osisRef="Gen.26.34">Gen 26:34</reference>; Adah is called Bashemath in the same place; and she who is here called Bashemath is called Mahalath, <reference osisRef="Gen.28.9">Gen 28:9</reference>. These are variations which cannot be easily accounted for; and they are not of sufficient importance to engross much time. It is well known that the same persons in Scripture are often called by different names. <div eID="gen1720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1721" type="x-p"/> Anah the daughter of Zibeon - But this same Anah is said to be the son of Zibeon, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.24">Gen 36:24</reference>, though in this and <reference osisRef="Gen.36.14">Gen 36:14</reference> he is said to be the daughter of Zibeon. But the Samaritan, the Septuagint, (and the Syriac, in <reference osisRef="Gen.36.2">Gen 36:2</reference>), read son instead of daughter, which Houbigant and Kennicott contend to be the true reading. Others say that daughter should be referred to Aholibamah, who was the daughter of Anah, and granddaughter of Zibeon. I should rather prefer the reading of the Samaritan, Septuagint, and Syriac, and read, both here and in <reference osisRef="Gen.36.14">Gen 36:14</reference>, "Aholibamah, the daughter of Anah the son of Zibeon," and then the whole will agree with <reference osisRef="Gen.36.24">Gen 36:24</reference>.
entries.c04805460ce3de22720875ce83f60f61a5a31b57: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen1721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1722" type="x-p"/> Esau took his wives, etc. - So it appears that Esau and Jacob dwelt together in Canaan, whither the former removed from Seir, probably soon after the return of Jacob. That they were on the most friendly footing this sufficiently proves; and Esau shows the same dignified conduct as on other occasions, in leaving Canaan to Jacob, and returning again to Mount Seir; certainly a much less fruitful region than that which he now in behalf of his brother voluntarily abandoned.
entries.206a99d663ffb915a645f4b2548098a422450e2a: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen1722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1723" type="x-p"/> Timna was concubine to Eliphaz - As Timna was sister to Lotan the Horite, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.22">Gen 36:22</reference>, we see how the family of Esau and the Horites got intermixed. This might give the sons of Esau a pretext to seize the land, and expel the ancient inhabitants, as we find they did, <reference osisRef="Deu.2.12">Deu 2:12</reference>. <div eID="gen1723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1724" type="x-p"/> Amalek - The father of the Amalekites, afterwards bitter enemies to the Jews, and whom God commanded to be entirely exterminated, <reference osisRef="Deu.25.17">Deu 25:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.25.19">Deu 25:19</reference>.
entries.97fc7ade4ad73f86c86cf83d4950464ca0c31cf0: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen1724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1725" type="x-p"/> Dukes of the sons of Esau - The word duke comes from the Latin dux, a captain or leader. The Hebrew אלוף alluph has the same signification; and as it is also the term for a thousand, which is a grand capital or leading number, probably the אלופי alluphey or dukes had this name from being leaders of or captains over a company of one thousand men; just as those among the Greeks called chiliarchs, which signifies the same; and as the Romans called those centurions who were captains over one hundred men, from the Latin word centum, which signifies a hundred. The ducal government was that which prevailed first among the Idumeans, or descendants of Esau. Here fourteen dukes are reckoned to Esau, seven that came of his wife, Adah, four of Bashemath, and three of Aholibamah.
entries.c05135487c8b43636e69243b815382901601341f: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen1725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1726" type="x-p"/> Duke Korah - This Dr. Kennicott pronounces to be an interpolation. "It is certain, from <reference osisRef="Gen.36.4">Gen 36:4</reference>, that Eliphaz was Esau's son by Adah; and from <reference osisRef="Gen.36.11">Gen 36:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.12">Gen 36:12</reference>, that Eliphaz had but six sons, Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, Kenaz, and Amalek. It is also certain, from <reference osisRef="Gen.36.5">Gen 36:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.14">Gen 36:14</reference>, that Korah was the son of Esau (not of Eliphaz) by Aholibamah; and as such he is properly mentioned in <reference osisRef="Gen.36.18">Gen 36:18</reference> : These are the sons of Aholibamah, Esau's wife: duke Jeush, duke Jaalam, Duke Korah. It is clear, therefore, that some transcriber has improperly inserted duke Korah in <reference osisRef="Gen.36.16">Gen 36:16</reference>; from which interpolation both the Samaritan text and the Samaritan version are free." - Kennicott's Remarks. Everything considered, I incline to the opinion that these words were not originally in the text.
entries.735a1c7c57a69374ba6e94c25ad0a502e60b00ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen1726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1727" type="x-p"/> These are the sons of Seir the Horite - These Horites were the original inhabitants of the country of Seir, called the land of the Horites, and afterwards the land of the Idumeans, when the descendants of Esau had driven them out. These people are first mentioned <reference osisRef="Gen.14.6">Gen 14:6</reference>.
entries.909b4ebdd73b87204593dfa885d33c1ee9eb82a2: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen1727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1728" type="x-p"/> These are the dukes of the Horites - It appears pretty evident that the Horites and the descendants of Esau were mixed together in the same land, as before observed; and Calmet has very properly remarked, that if we compare this verse with <reference osisRef="Gen.36.30">Gen 36:30</reference>, there were princes of Seir in the country of Seir, and in that of Edom; and in comparing the generations of Seir and Esau, we are obliged to consider these princes as contemporary.
entries.0e1bd03691e6da79e48edcf714446874a67e093c: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen1728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1729" type="x-p"/> This was that Anah that found the mules in the wilderness - The words את הימם eth kaiyemim, here translated mules, has given rise to a great variety of conjectures and discordant opinions. St. Jerome, who renders it aquas calidas, warm springs, or hot baths, says there are as many opinions concerning it as there are commentators. <div eID="gen1729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1730" type="x-p"/> The Septuagint has τον Ιαμειν, which seems to be the name of a man; but this is expressed in a great variety of ways in different MSS. of that version. <div eID="gen1730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1731" type="x-p"/> The Syriac renders it mayé, waters; the author of this version having read in the Hebrew copy from which he translated. מים mayim, waters, for ימם yemim, the two first letters being transposed. <div eID="gen1731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1732" type="x-p"/> Onkelos translates the word גבריא gibbaraiya, giants, or strong or powerful men. <div eID="gen1732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1733" type="x-p"/> The Samaritan text has haaimim, and the Samaritan version am aimai, the Emim, a warlike people, bordering upon the Horites. <div eID="gen1733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1734" type="x-p"/> The Targum of Jonathan ben Uzziel paraphrases the place thus: "This is the Anah who united the onager with the tame ass, and in process of time he found mules produced by them." R. D. Kimchi says, that "Zibeon was both the father and brother of Anah; and this Anah, intent on heterogeneous mixtures, caused asses and horses to copulate, and so produced mules." R. S. Jarchi is of the same opinion. See his comment on this place. <div eID="gen1734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1735" type="x-p"/> Bochart believes the Emim are meant; and argues forcibly, 1. That מצא matsa, he found, never signifies to invent, but rather the meeting with or happening on a thing which already exists. 2. That mules are never called ימם yemim in the Scriptures, but פרדים peradim. 3. That Anah fed Asses only, not horses. And, 4. That there is no mention of mules in Palestine till the days of David. From the whole he concludes that the Emim are meant, with whom Anah fought; and he brings many places of Scripture where the same form of expression, he or they found, signifies the onset to battle, <reference osisRef="Jdg.1.5">Jdg 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.3">1Sam 31:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.24">1Kgs 13:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.22.8">2Chr 22:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.35.27">Num 35:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.4.14">Gen 4:14</reference>; with many others. See the Hierozoicon, vol. i., cap. 21, p. 23S., edit. 1692. <div eID="gen1735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1736" type="x-p"/> Gusset, in Comment. Heb. Ling., examines what Bochart has asserted, and supposes that mules, not the Emim, were found by Anah. <div eID="gen1736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1737" type="x-p"/> Wagenseil would credit what Bochart has asserted, did not stronger reasons lead him to believe that the word means a sort of plant! <div eID="gen1737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1738" type="x-p"/> From the above opinions and versions the reader may choose which he likes best, or invent one for himself. My own opinion is, that mules were not known before the time of Anah; and that he was probably the first who coupled the mare and ass together to produce this mongrel, or the first who met with creatures of this race in some very secluded part of the wilderness. Is it not probable that from this Anah, or ענה enah, the Enetae derived at least their fabulous origin, whom Homer mentions as famous for their race of wild mules? Παφλαγονων δ' ἡγειτο Πυλαιμενεος λασιον κηρ, Εξ Ενετων, ὁθεν ἡμιονων γενος αγροτεραων. <div eID="gen1738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1739" type="x-p"/> IL., lib. ii., v. 852. <div eID="gen1739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1740" type="x-p"/> The Paphlagonians Pylaemenes rules, <div eID="gen1740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1741" type="x-p"/> Where rich Henetia breeds her Savage Mules. <div eID="gen1741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1742" type="x-p"/> Pope. <div eID="gen1742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1743" type="x-p"/> The Enetae or Henetae, who were a people contiguous to Paphlagonia, Cappadocia, and Galatia, might have derived their origin from this Anah, or Henah, out of which the Ενετοι of the ancient Greek writers might have been formed; and according to Theophrastus, Strabo, and Plutarch, the first mules were seen among these people. See Ludov, De Dieu and Scheuchzer.
entries.55f3595666c177d48929eff5b13c4221b88217ef: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen1743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1744" type="x-p"/> Before there reigned any king over - Israel - I suppose all the verses, from <reference osisRef="Gen.36.31-Gen.36.39">Gen 36:31-39</reference> inclusive, have been transferred to this place from <reference osisRef="1Chr.1.43-1Chr.1.50">1Chr 1:43-50</reference>, as it is not likely they could have been written by Moses; and it is quite possible they might have been, at a very early period, written in the margin of an authentic copy, to make out the regal succession in Edom, prior to the consecration of Saul; which words being afterwards found in the margin of a valuable copy, from which others were transcribed, were supposed by the copyist to be a part of the text, which having been omitted by the mistake of the original writer, had been since added to make up the deficiency; on this conviction he would not hesitate to transcribe them consecutively in his copy. In most MSS. sentences and paragraphs have been left out by the copyists, which, when perceived, have been added in the margin, either by the original writer, or by some later hand. Now, as the margin was the ordinary place where glosses or explanatory notes were written, it is easy to conceive how the notes, as well as the parts of the original text found in the margin, might be all incorporated with the text by a future transcriber; and his MSS., being often copied, would of course multiply the copies with such additions, as we have much reason to believe has been the case. This appears very frequently in the Vulgate and Septuagint; and an English Bible now before me written some time in the fourteenth century, exhibits several proofs of this principle. See the preface to this work. <div eID="gen1744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1745" type="x-p"/> I know there is another way of accounting for those words on the ground of their being written originally by Moses; but to me it is not satisfactory. It is simply this: the word king should be considered as implying any kind of regular government, whether by chiefs, dukes, judges, etc., and therefore when Moses says these are the kings which reigned in Edom, before there was any king in Israel, he may be only understood as saying that these kings reigned among the Edomites before the family of Jacob had acquired any considerable power, or before the time in which his twelve sons had become the fathers of those numerous tribes, at the head of which, as king himself in Jeshurun, he now stood. <div eID="gen1745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1746" type="x-p"/> Esau, after his dukes, had eight kings, who reigned successively over their people, while Israel were in affliction in Egypt.
entries.ccee700644fef4842fa6295e4162058e5fe583e0: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen1746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1747" type="x-p"/> Jobab the son of Zerah - Many have supposed that Jobab is the same as Job, so remarkable for his afflictions and patience; and that Eliphaz, mentioned <reference osisRef="Gen.36.10">Gen 36:10</reference>, etc., was the same who in the book of Job is called one of his friends: but there is no proper proof of this, and there are many reasons against it.
entries.e31f3d39b529b0dbd28960ef3af10e1cfb77d1bc: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen1747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1748" type="x-p"/> Smote Midian in the field of Moab - Bishop Cumberland supposes that this was Midian, the son of Abraham by Keturah, and that he was killed by Hadad some time before he was one hundred and nine years of age; and that Moses recorded this, probably, because it was a calamity to the ancestor of Jethro, his father-in-law - Orig. of Nat., p. 14.
entries.e4d373042c55f26f614d72c6468ed47d2c55cb94: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen1748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1749" type="x-p"/> These are the names of the dukes that came of Esau - These dukes did not govern the whole nation of the Idumeans, but they were chiefs in their respective families, in their places - the districts they governed, and to which they gave their names. Calmet thinks that those mentioned above were dukes in Edom or Idumea at the time of the exodus of Israel from Egypt.
entries.38d14e34fb4d91536360de6ec29573d6a8d8006c: <hi type="bold">Verse 43</hi> <div eID="gen1749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1750" type="x-p"/> He is Esau the father of the Edomites - That is, The preceding list contains an account of the posterity of Esau, who was the father of Edom. Thus ends Esau's history; for after this there is no farther account of his life, actions, or death, in the Pentateuch. <div eID="gen1750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1751" type="x-p"/> 1. As Esau is so considerable a person in polemic divinity, it may be necessary, in this place especially, to say something farther of his conduct and character. I have already, in several places, endeavored, and I hope successfully, to wipe off the odium that has been thrown upon this man, (see the notes on Genesis 27 (note) and Genesis 33 (note))., without attempting to lessen his faults; and the unprejudiced reader must see that, previously to this last account we have of him, his character stands without a blot, except in the case of selling his birthright, and his purpose to destroy his brother. To the first he was led by his famishing situation and the unkindness of his brother, who refused to save his life but on this condition; and the latter, made in the heat of vexation and passion, he never attempted to execute, even when he had the most ample means and the fairest opportunity to do it. <div eID="gen1751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1752" type="x-p"/> Dr. Shuckford has drawn an impartial character of Esau, from which I extract the following particulars: "Esau was a plain, generous, and honest man, for we have no reason, from any thing that appears in his life or actions, to think him wicked beyond other men of his age or times; and his generous and good temper appears from all his behavior towards his brother. When they first met he was all humanity and affection, and he had no uneasiness when he found that Jacob followed him not to Seir, but went to live near his father. And at Isaac's death we do not find that he made any difficulty of quitting Canaan, which was the very point which, if he had harbored any latent (evil) intentions, would have revived all his resentments. He is indeed called in Scripture the profane Esau; and it is written, Jacob have I loved, and Esau have I hated; but there is, I think, no reason to infer, from any of those expressions, that Esau was a very wicked man, or that God hated or punished him for an immoral life. For, 1. The sentence here against him is said expressly to be founded, not upon his actions, for it was determined before the children had done good or evil. 2. God's hatred of Esau was not a hatred which induced him to punish him with any evil, for he was as happy in all the blessings of this life as either Abraham, Isaac, or Jacob; and his posterity had a land designed by God to be their possession, as well as the children of Jacob, and they were put in possession of it much sooner than the Israelites; and God was pleased to protect them in the enjoyment of it, and to caution the Israelites against invading them with a remarkable strictness, <reference osisRef="Deu.2.4">Deu 2:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.2.5">Deu 2:5</reference>. And as God was pleased thus to bless Esau and his children in the blessings of this life, even as much as he blessed Abraham, Isaac, or Jacob, if not more, why may we not hope to find him with them at the last day, as well as Lot or Job or any other good and virtuous man, who was not designed to be a partaker of the blessing given to Abraham? 3. All the punishment inflicted on Esau was an exclusion from being heir to the blessing promised to Abraham and to his seed, which was a favor not granted to Lot, to Job, to several other very virtuous and good men. 4. St. Paul, in the passage before cited, only intends to show the Jews that God had all along given the favors that led to the Messiah where he pleased; to Abraham, not to Lot; to Jacob, not to Esau; as at the time St. Paul wrote the Gentiles were made the people of God, not the Jews. 5. Esau is indeed called profane, (βεβηλος), but I think that word does not mean wicked or immoral, ασεβης or ἁμαρτωλος· he was called profane for not having that due value for the priest's office which he should have had; and therefore, though I think it does not appear that he was cut off from being the heir of the promises by any particular action in his life, yet his turn of mind and thoughts do appear to have been such as to evidence that God's purpose towards Jacob was founded on the truest wisdom." - Shuckford's Connections, vol. ii., p.174, etc. <div eID="gen1752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1753" type="x-p"/> The truth is, the Messiah must spring from some One family, and God chose Abraham's through Isaac, Jacob, etc., rather than the same through Ishmael, Esau, and the others in that line; but from this choice it does not follow that the first were all necessarily saved, and the others necessarily lost. <div eID="gen1753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1754" type="x-p"/> 2. To some the genealogical lists in this chapter will doubtless appear uninteresting, especially those which concern Esau and his descendants; but it was as necessary to register the generations of Esau as to register those of Jacob, in order to show that the Messiah did not spring from the former, but that he did spring from the latter. The genealogical tables, so frequently met with in the sacred writings, and so little regarded by Christians in general, are extremely useful. 1. As they are standing proofs of the truth of the prophecies, which stated that the Messiah should come from a particular family, which prophecies were clearly fulfilled in the birth of Christ. 2. As they testify, to the conviction of the Jews, that the Messiah thus promised is found in the person of Jesus of Nazareth, who incontestably sprang from the last, the only remaining branch of the family of David. These registers were religiously preserved among the Jews till the destruction of Jerusalem, after which they were all destroyed, insomuch that there is not a Jew in the universe who can trace himself to the family of David; consequently, all expectation of a Messiah to come is, even on their own principles, nugatory and absurd, as nothing remains to legitimate his birth. When Christ came all these registers were in existence. When St. Matthew and St. Luke wrote, all these registers were still in existence; and had they pretended what could not have been supported, an appeal to the registers would have convicted them of a falsehood. But no Jew attempted to do this, notwithstanding the excess of their malice against Christ and his followers; and because they did not do it, we may safely assert no Jew could do it. Thus the foundation standeth sure.  <chapter eID="Gen.36"/> <div eID="gen1754" type="x-p"/>

entries.212aaaa4701b3b423148ce966f06f115728c28cd: <reference osisRef="Gen.36.1-Gen.36.8">Gen 36:1-8</reference> <div eID="gen420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen421" type="x-p"/> Esau’s Wives and Children. His Settlement in the Mountains of Seir. - In the heading (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.1">Gen 36:1</reference>) the surname <hi type="italic">Edom</hi> is added to the name Esau, which he received at his birth, because the former became the national designation of his descendants. - <reference osisRef="Gen.36.2">Gen 36:2</reference>, Gen 36:3. The names of Esau’s three wives differ from those given in the previous accounts (<reference osisRef="Gen.26.34">Gen 26:34</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.28.9">Gen 28:9</reference>), and in one instance the father’s name as well. The daughter of Elon the Hittite is called <hi type="italic">Adah</hi> (the ornament), and in <reference osisRef="Gen.26.34">Gen 26:34</reference> <hi type="italic">Basmath</hi> (the fragrant); the second is called <hi type="italic">Aholibamah</hi> (probably tent-height), the daughter of Anah, daughter, i.e., grand-daughter of Zibeon the Hivite, and in <reference osisRef="Gen.26.34">Gen 26:34</reference>, <hi type="italic">Jehudith</hi> (the praised or praiseworthy), daughter of Beeri the Hittite; the third, the daughter of Ishmael, is called <hi type="italic">Basmath</hi> here and <hi type="italic">Mahalath</hi> in Gen 28:9. This difference arose from the fact, that Moses availed himself of genealogical documents for Esau’s family and tribe, and inserted them without alteration. It presents no irreconcilable discrepancy, therefore, but may be explained from the ancient custom in the East, of giving surnames, as the Arabs frequently do still, founded upon some important or memorable event in a man’s life, which gradually superseded the other name (e.g., the name Edom, as explained in <reference osisRef="Gen.25.30">Gen 25:30</reference>); whilst as a rule the women received new names when they were married (cf. Chardin, Hengstenberg, <hi type="italic">Dissertations</hi>, vol. ii. p. 223-6). The different names given for the father of Aholibamah or Judith, Hengstenberg explains by referring to the statement in <reference osisRef="Gen.36.24">Gen 36:24</reference>, that Anah, the son of Zibeon, while watching the asses of his father in the desert, discovered the warm springs (of Calirrhoe), on which he founds the acute conjecture, that from this discovery Anah received the surname <hi type="italic">Beeri</hi>, i.e., spring-man, which so threw his original name into the shade, as to be the only name given in the genealogical table. There is no force in the objection, that according to <reference osisRef="Gen.36.25">Gen 36:25</reference> Aholibamah was not a daughter of the discoverer of the springs, but of his uncle of the same name. For where is it stated that the Aholibamah mentioned in <reference osisRef="Gen.36.25">Gen 36:25</reference> was Esau’s wife? And is it a thing unheard of that aunt and niece should have the same name? If Zibeon gave his second son the name of his brother Anah (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.36.24">Gen 36:24</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.36.20">Gen 36:20</reference>), why could not his son Anah have named his daughter after his cousin, the daughter of his father’s brother? The reception of Aholibamah into the list of the Seirite princes is no proof that she was Esau’s wife, but may be much more naturally supposed to have arisen from the same (unknown) circumstance as that which caused one of the seats of the Edomitish <hi type="italic">Alluphim</hi> to be called by her name (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.41">Gen 36:41</reference>). - Lastly, the remaining diversity, viz., that Anah is called a Hivite in <reference osisRef="Gen.36.2">Gen 36:2</reference> and a Hittite in <reference osisRef="Gen.26.34">Gen 26:34</reference>, is not to be explained by the conjecture, that for Hivite we should read Horite, according to <reference osisRef="Gen.36.20">Gen 36:20</reference>, but by the simple assumption that Hittite is used in <reference osisRef="Gen.26.34">Gen 26:34</reference> <hi type="italic">sensu latiori</hi> for Canaanite, according to the analogy of <reference osisRef="Josh.1.4">Jos 1:4</reference>; 1Ki 10:29; 2Ki 7:6; just as the two Hittite wives of Esau are called daughters of Canaan in Gen 28:8. For the historical account, the general name Hittite sufficed; but the genealogical list required the special name of the particular branch of the Canaanitish tribes, viz., the Hivites. In just as simple a manner may the introduction of the Hivite Zibeon among the Horites of Seir (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.20">Gen 36:20</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.36.24">Gen 36:24</reference>) be explained, viz., on the supposition that the removed to the mountains of Seir, and there became a Horite, i.e., a troglodyte, or dweller in a cave. - The names of Esau’s sons occur again in 1Ch 1:35. The statement in <reference osisRef="Gen.36.6">Gen 36:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.7">Gen 36:7</reference>, that Esau went with his family and possessions, which he had acquired in Canaan, into the land of Seir, from before his brother Jacob, does not imply (in contradiction to <reference osisRef="Gen.32.4">Gen 32:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.33.14-Gen.33.16">Gen 33:14-16</reference>) that he did not leave the land of Canaan till after Jacob’s return. The words may be understood without difficulty as meaning, that after founding a house of his own, when his family and flocks increased, Esau sought a home in Seir, because he knew that Jacob, as the heir, would enter upon the family possessions, but without waiting till he returned and actually took possession. In the clause “<hi type="italic">went into the country</hi>” (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.6">Gen 36:6</reference>), the name <hi type="italic">Seir</hi> or <hi type="italic">Edom</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.36.16">Gen 36:16</reference>) must have dropt out, as the words “into the country” convey no sense when standing by themselves.
entries.70c4c065826270ba68f73bc5e78a6d8e96a38915: <reference osisRef="Gen.36.9-Gen.36.14">Gen 36:9-14</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.1.36-1Chr.1.37">1Ch 1:36-37</reference>). Esau’s Sons and Grandsons as Fathers of Tribes. - Through them he became the <hi type="italic">father of Edom</hi>, i.e., the founder of the Edomitish nation on the mountains of Seir. <hi type="italic">Mouth Seir</hi> is the mountainous region between the Dead Sea and the Elanitic Gulf, the northern half of which is called <hi type="italic">Jebâl</hi> (Γεβαλήνη) by the Arabs, the southern half, <hi type="italic">Sherah</hi> (Rob. <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> ii. 552). - In the case of two of the wives of Esau, who bore only one son each, the tribes were founded not by the sons, but by the grandsons; but in that of Aholibamah the three sons were the founders. Among the sons of Eliphaz we find <hi type="italic">Amalek</hi>, whose mother was Timna, the concubine of Eliphaz. He was the ancestor of the Amalekites, who attacked the Israelites at Horeb as they came out of Egypt under Moses (Exo 17:8.), and not merely of a mixed tribe of Amalekites and Edomites, belonging to the supposed aboriginal Amalekite nation. For the Arabic legend of <hi type="italic">Amlik</hi> as an aboriginal tribe of Arabia is far too recent, confused, and contradictory to counterbalance the clear testimony of the record before us. The allusion to the fields of the Amalekites in <reference osisRef="Gen.14.7">Gen 14:7</reference> does not imply that the tribe was in existence in Abraham’s time, nor does the expression “first of the nations,” in the saying of Balaam (Num 24:20), represent Amalek as the aboriginal or oldest tribe, but simply as the first heathen tribe by which Israel was attacked. The Old Testament says nothing of any fusion of Edomites or Horites with Amalekites, nor does it mention a double Amalek (cf. Hengstenberg, <hi type="italic">Dissertations</hi> 2, 247ff., and Kurtz, <hi type="italic">History</hi> i. 122, 3, ii. 240ff.).<note placement="foot">The occurrence of “Timna and Amalek” in <reference osisRef="1Chr.1.36">1Ch 1:36</reference>, as coordinate with the sons of Eliphaz, is simply a more concise form of saying “and from Timna, Amalek.”</note> <div eID="gen421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen422" type="x-p"/> If there had been an Amalek previous to Edom, with the important part which they took in opposition to Israel even in the time of Moses, the book of Genesis would not have omitted to give their pedigree in the list of the nations. At a very early period the Amalekites separated from the other tribes of Edom and formed an independent people, having their headquarters in the southern part of the mountains of Judah, as far as Kadesh (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.7">Gen 14:7</reference>; Num 13:29; Num 14:43, Num 14:45), but, like the Bedouins, spreading themselves as a nomad tribe over the whole of the northern portion of Arabia Petraea, from Havilah to Shur on the border of Egypt (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.3">1Sa 15:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.7">1Sa 15:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.8">1Sa 27:8</reference>); whilst one branch penetrated into the heart of Canaan, so that a range of hills, in what was afterwards the inheritance of Ephraim, bore the name of mountains of the Amalekites (Jdg 12:15, cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.5.14">Gen 5:14</reference>). Those who settled in Arabia seem also to have separated in the course of time into several branches, so that Amalekite hordes invaded the land of Israel in connection sometimes with the Midianites and the sons of the East (the Arabs, Jdg 6:3; Jdg 7:12), and at other times with the Ammonites (Jdg 3:13). After they had been defeated by Saul (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.48">1Sa 14:48</reference>; 1Sa 15:2.), and frequently chastised by David (<reference osisRef="1Sam.27.8">1Sa 27:8</reference>; 1Sa 30:1.; <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.12">2Sa 8:12</reference>), the remnant of them was exterminated under Hezekiah by the Simeonites on the mountains of Seir (<reference osisRef="1Chr.4.42-1Chr.4.43">1Ch 4:42-43</reference>).
entries.999830ec51331e991f737b7a11e354fd5bd6567f: <reference osisRef="Gen.36.15-Gen.36.19">Gen 36:15-19</reference> <div eID="gen422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen423" type="x-p"/> The Tribe-Princes Who Descended from Esau. - אלּוּפים was the distinguishing title of the Edomite and Horite phylarchs; and it is only incidentally that it is applied to Jewish heads of tribes in Zec 9:7, and Zec 12:5. It is probably derived from אלף or אלפים, equivalent to משׁפּחות, families (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.19">1Sa 10:19</reference>; Mic 5:2), - the heads of the families, i.e., of the principal divisions, of the tribe. The names of these <hi type="italic">Alluphim</hi> are not names of places, but of persons-of the three sons and ten grandsons of Esau mentioned in <reference osisRef="Gen.36.9-Gen.36.14">Gen 36:9-14</reference>; though <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> would reverse the process and interpret the whole geographically. - In <reference osisRef="Gen.36.16">Gen 36:16</reference> <hi type="italic">Korah</hi> has probably been copied by mistake from <reference osisRef="Gen.36.18">Gen 36:18</reference>, and should therefore be erased, as it really is in the <hi type="italic">Samar</hi>. Codex.
entries.bbaf163fbd8a7a258a3d08871ea438432b8e1d1d: <reference osisRef="Gen.36.20-Gen.36.29">Gen 36:20-29</reference> (parallel, <reference osisRef="1Chr.1.38-1Chr.1.42">1Ch 1:38-42</reference>). Descendants of Seir the Horite; - the inhabitants of the land, or pre-Edomitish population of the country. - “<hi type="italic">The Horite:</hi>” ὁ Τρωγλοδύτης, the dweller in caves, which abound in the mountains of Edom (vid., Rob. <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> ii. p. 424). The Horites, who had previously been an independent people (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.6">Gen 14:6</reference>), were partly exterminated and partly subjugated by the descendants of Esau (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.12">Deu 2:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.2.22">Deu 2:22</reference>). Seven sons of Seir are given as tribe-princes of the Horites, who are afterwards mentioned as <hi type="italic">Alluphim</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.29">Gen 36:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.30">Gen 36:30</reference>), also their sons, as well as two daughters, <hi type="italic">Timna</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.22">Gen 36:22</reference>) and <hi type="italic">Aholibamah</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.25">Gen 36:25</reference>), who obtained notoriety from the face that two of the headquarters of Edomitish tribe-princes bore their names (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.40">Gen 36:40</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.36.41">Gen 36:41</reference>). <hi type="italic">Timna</hi> was probably the same as the concubine of Eliphaz (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.12">Gen 36:12</reference>); but <hi type="italic">Aholibamah</hi> was not the wife of Esau (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.36.2">Gen 36:2</reference>). - There are a few instances in which the names in this list differ from those in the Chronicles. But they are differences which either consist of variation in form, or have arisen from mistakes in copying.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> also undertakes to explain these names geographically, and to point them out in tribes and places of Arabia, assuming, quite arbitrarily and in opposition to the text, that the names refer to tribes, not to persons, although an incident is related of Zibeon’s son, which proves at once that the list relates to persons and not to tribes; and expecting his readers to believe that not only are the descendants of these troglodytes, who were exterminated before the time of Moses, still to be found, but even their names may be traced in certain Bedouin tribes, though more than 3000 years have passed away! The utter groundlessness of such explanations, which rest upon nothing more than similarity of names, may be seen in the association of <hi type="italic">Shobal</hi> with <hi type="italic">Syria Sobal</hi> (Judith 3:1), the name used by the Crusaders for <hi type="italic">Arabia tertia</hi>, i.e., the southernmost district below the Dead Sea, which was conquered by them. For notwithstanding the resemblance of the name <hi type="italic">Shobal</hi> to <hi type="italic">Sobal</hi>, no one could seriously think of connecting <hi type="italic">Syria Sobal</hi> with the Horite prince <hi type="italic">Shobal</hi>, unless he was altogether ignorant of the apocryphal origin of the former name, which first of all arose from the Greek or Latin version of the Old Testament, and in fact from a misunderstanding of <reference osisRef="Ps.60.2">Psa 60:2</reference>, where, instead צובה ארם, <hi type="italic">Aram</hi> <hi type="italic">Zobah</hi>, we find in the lxx Συριά Σοβάλ, and in the <hi type="italic">Vulg</hi>. <hi type="italic">Syria et Sobal</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen424" type="x-p"/> Of <hi type="italic">Anah</hi>, the son of Zibeon, it is related (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.24">Gen 36:24</reference>), that as he fed the asses of his father in the desert, he “found היּמם” - not “he invented mules,” as the Talmud, Luther, etc., render it, for mules are פּרדים, and מצא does not mean to invent; but he discovered <hi type="italic">aquae calidae</hi> (<hi type="italic">Vulg</hi>.), either the hot sulphur spring of <hi type="italic">Calirrhoe</hi> in the Wady <hi type="italic">Zerka Maein</hi> (vid., <reference osisRef="Gen.10.19">Gen 10:19</reference>), or those in the Wady <hi type="italic">el Ahsa</hi> to the S.E. of the Dead Sea, or those in the Wady <hi type="italic">Hamad</hi> between Kerek and the Dead Sea.<note placement="foot">It is possible that there may be something significant in the fact that it was “as he was feeding his father’s asses,” and that the asses may have contributed to the discovery; just as the whirlpool of Karlsbad is said to have been discovered through a hound of Charles IV, which pursued a stag into a hot spring, and attracted the huntsmen to the spot by its howling.</note>
entries.8ec5d52d1eef6b041795223e9eaadff8d54f5e71: <reference osisRef="Gen.36.30">Gen 36:30</reference> <div eID="gen424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen425" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">These are the princes of the Horites according to their princes,</hi>” i.e., as their princes were individually named in the land of Seir. ל in enumerations indicates the relation of the individual to the whole, and of the whole to the individual.
entries.79c2ed736ec0a16f489d985f2b4f14cf6ca84fc9: <reference osisRef="Gen.36.31-Gen.36.39">Gen 36:31-39</reference> (Parallel, <reference osisRef="1Chr.1.43-1Chr.1.50">1Ch 1:43-50</reference>). The Kings in the Land of Edom: before the children of Israel had a king. It is to be observed in connection with the eight kings mentioned here, that whilst they follow one another, that is to say, one never comes to the throne till his predecessor is dead, yet the son never succeeds the father, but they all belong to different families and places, and in the case of the last the statement that “he died” is wanting. From this it is unquestionably obvious, that the sovereignty was elective; that the kings were chosen by the phylarchs; and, as <reference osisRef="Isa.34.12">Isa 34:12</reference> also shows, that they lived or reigned contemporaneously with these. The contemporaneous existence of the <hi type="italic">Alluphim</hi> and the kings may also be inferred from <reference osisRef="Exod.15.15">Exo 15:15</reference> as compared with Num 20:14. Whilst it was with the king of Edom that Moses treated respecting the passage through the land, in the song of Moses it is the princes who tremble with fear on account of the miraculous passage through the Red Sea (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.29">Eze 32:29</reference>). Lastly, this is also supported by the fact, that the account of the seats of the phylarchs (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.40-Gen.36.43">Gen 36:40-43</reference>) follows the list of the kings. This arrangement would have been thoroughly unsuitable if the monarchy had been founded upon the ruins of the phylarchs (vid., Hengstenberg, <hi type="italic">ut sup</hi>. pp. 238ff.). Of all the kings of Edom, not one is named elsewhere. It is true, the attempt has been made to identify the fourth, <hi type="italic">Hadad</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.35">Gen 36:35</reference>), with the Edomite Hadad who rose up against Solomon (1Ki 11:14); but without foundation. The contemporary of Solomon was of royal blood, but neither a king nor a pretender; our Hadad, on the contrary, was a king, but he was the son of an unknown Hadad of the town of <hi type="italic">Avith</hi>, and no relation to his predecessor <hi type="italic">Husham</hi> of the country of the Temanites. It is related of him that he smote Midian in the fields of Moab (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.35">Gen 36:35</reference>); from which Hengstenberg (pp. 235-6) justly infers that this event cannot have been very remote from the Mosaic age, since we find the Midianites allied to the Moabites in Num 22; ; whereas afterwards, viz., in the time of Gideon, the Midianites vanished from history, and in Solomon’s days the fields of Moab, being Israelitish territory, cannot have served as a field of battle for the Midianites and Moabites. - Of the tribe-cities of these kings only a few can be identified now. <hi type="italic">Bozrah</hi>, a noted city of the Edomites (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.6">Isa 34:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.1">Isa 43:1</reference>, etc.), is still to be traced in el Buseireh, a village with ruins in <hi type="italic">Jebal</hi> (Rob. <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> ii. 571). - The land of the <hi type="italic">Temanite</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.34">Gen 36:34</reference>) is a province in northern Idumaea, with a city, Teman, which has not yet been discovered; according to <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi>, <hi type="italic">quinque millibus</hi> from Petra. - <hi type="italic">Rehoboth</hi> of the river (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.37">Gen 36:37</reference>) can neither be the Idumaean <hi type="italic">Robotha</hi>, nor <hi type="italic">er Ruheibeh</hi> in the wady running towards <hi type="italic">el Arish</hi>, but must be sought for on the Euphrates, say in <hi type="italic">Errachabi</hi> or <hi type="italic">Rachabeh</hi>, near the mouth of the Chaboras. Consequently Saul, who sprang from Rehoboth, was a foreigner. - Of the last king, <hi type="italic">Hadar</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.39">Gen 36:39</reference>; not Hadad, as it is written in <reference osisRef="1Chr.1.50">1Ch 1:50</reference>), the wife, the mother-in-law, and the mother are mentioned: his death is not mentioned here, but is added by the later chronicler (<reference osisRef="1Chr.1.51">1Ch 1:51</reference>). This can be explained easily enough from the simple fact, that at the time when the table was first drawn up, Hadad was still alive and seated upon the throne. In all probability, therefore, Hadad was the king of Edom, to whom Moses applied for permission to pass through the land (Num 20:14.).<note placement="foot">If this be admitted; then, on the supposition that this list of kings contains all the previous kings of Edom, the introduction of monarchy among the Edomites can hardly have taken place more than 200 years before the Exodus; and, in that case, none of the phylarchs named in <reference osisRef="Gen.36.15-Gen.36.18">Gen 36:15-18</reference> can have lived to see its establishment. For the list only reaches to the grandsons of Esau, none of whom are likely to have lived more than 100 or 150 years after Esau’s death. It is true we do not know when Esau died; but 413 years elapsed between the death of Jacob and the Exodus, and Joseph, who was born in the 91st years of Jacob’s life, died 54 years afterwards, i.e., 359 years before the Exodus. But Esau was married in his 40th year, 37 years before Jacob (<reference osisRef="Gen.26.34">Gen 26:34</reference>), and had sons and daughters before his removal to Seir (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.6">Gen 36:6</reference>). Unless, therefore, his sons and grandsons attained a most unusual age, or were married remarkably late in life, his grandsons can hardly have outlived Joseph more than 100 years. Now, if we fix their death at about 250 years before the Exodus of Israel from Egypt, there remains from that point to the arrival of the Israelites at the land of Edom (Num 20:14) a period of 290 years; amply sufficient for the reigns of eight kings, even if the monarchy was not introduced till after the death of the last of the phylarchs mentioned in <reference osisRef="Gen.36.15">Gen 36:15</reference>-18.</note> <div eID="gen425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen426" type="x-p"/> At any rate the list is evidently a record relating to the Edomitish kings of a pre-Mosaic age. But if this is the case, the heading, “<hi type="italic">These are the kings that reigned in the land of Edom, before there reigned any king over the children of Israel,</hi>” does not refer to the time when the monarchy was introduced into Israel under Saul, but was written with the promise in mind, that kings should come out of the loins of Jacob (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.11">Gen 35:11</reference>, cf. Gen 17:4.), and merely expresses the thought, that Edom became a kingdom at an earlier period than Israel. Such a thought was by no means inappropriate to the Mosaic age. For the idea, “that Israel was destined to grow into a kingdom with monarchs of his own family, was a hope handed down to the age of Moses, which the long residence in Egypt was well adapted to foster” (<hi type="italic">Del</hi>.).
entries.2e170a3db16f4cfb55db1c7a04337ffd9d10e505: <reference osisRef="Gen.36.40-Gen.36.43">Gen 36:40-43</reference> (Parallel, <reference osisRef="1Chr.1.51-1Chr.1.54">1Ch 1:51-54</reference>). Seats of the Tribe-Princes of Esau According to Their Families. - That the names which follow are not a second list of Edomitish tribe-princes (viz., of those who continued the ancient constitution, with its hereditary aristocracy, after Hadar’s death), but merely relate to the capital cities of the old phylarchs, is evident from the expression in the heading, “<hi type="italic">After their places, by their names,</hi>” as compared with <reference osisRef="Gen.36.43">Gen 36:43</reference>, “<hi type="italic">According to their habitations in the land of their possession</hi>.” This being the substance and intention of the list, there is nothing surprising in the fact, that out of the eleven names only two correspond to those given in <reference osisRef="Gen.36.15">Gen 36:15</reference>-19. This proves nothing more than that only two of the capitals received their names from the princes who captured or founded them, viz., <hi type="italic">Timnah</hi> and <hi type="italic">Kenaz</hi>. Neither of these has been discovered yet. The name <hi type="italic">Aholibamah</hi> is derived from the Horite princess (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.25">Gen 36:25</reference>); its site is unknown. <hi type="italic">Elah</hi> is the port <hi type="italic">Aila</hi> (vid., <reference osisRef="Gen.14.6">Gen 14:6</reference>). <hi type="italic">Pinon</hi> is the same as <hi type="italic">Phunon</hi>, an encampment of the Israelites (Num 33:42-43), celebrated for its mines, in which many Christians were condemned to labour under Diocletian, between Petra and Zoar, to the northeast of Wady Musa. <hi type="italic">Teman</hi> is the capital of the land of the Temanites (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.34">Gen 36:34</reference>). <hi type="italic">Mibzar</hi> is supposed by <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> to be Petra; but this is called <hi type="italic">Selah</hi> elsewhere (2Ki 14:7). <hi type="italic">Magdiel</hi> and <hi type="italic">Iram</hi> cannot be identified. The concluding sentence, “<hi type="italic">This is Esau, the father</hi> (founder) <hi type="italic">of Edom</hi>” (i.e., from his sprang the great nation of the Edomites, with its princes and kings, upon the mountains of Seir), not only terminates this section, but prepared the way for the history of Jacob, which commences with the following chapter.  <chapter eID="Gen.36"/> <div eID="gen426" type="x-p"/>

entries.0c77f212775e3cd283b6239a3832107351542e5c: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.36.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.36.1" sID="gen4651" type="section"/> <div sID="gen4652" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">Now these are the generations of Esau</hi>. Though Esau was an alien from the Church in the sight of God; yet since he also, as a son of Isaac, was favored with a temporal blessing, Moses celebrates his race, and inscribes a sufficiently lengthened catalogue of the people born from him. This commemoration, however, resembles an honorable sepulture. For although Esau, with his posterity, took the precedence; yet this dignity was like a bubble, which is comprised under the figure of the world, and which quickly perishes. As, therefore, it has been before said of other profane nations, so now Esau is exalted as on a lofty theater. But since there is no permanent condition out of the kingdom of God, the splendor attributed to him is evanescent, and the whole of his pomp departs like the passing scene of the stage. The Holy Spirit designed, indeed, to testify that the prophecy which Isaac uttered concerning Esau was not vain; but he has no sooner shown its effect, than he turns away our eyes, as if he had cast a veil over it, that we may confine our attention to the race of Jacob. Now, though Esau had children by three wives, in whom afterwards the blessing of God shone forth, yet polygamy is not, on that account, approved, nor the impure lust of man excused: but in this the goodness of God is rather to be admired, which, contrary to the order of nature, gave a good issue to evil beginnings.<div eID="gen4652" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.36.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen4651" osisID="Gen.36.1" type="section"/>
entries.1eb6bb66b3edf91b21f41db94f3f52fde6a8e1ea: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.36.6" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.36.6" sID="gen4653" type="section"/> <div sID="gen4654" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">6.</hi> <hi type="italic">And went into the country from the face of his brother Jacob</hi>. Moses does not mean that Esau departed purposely to give place to his brother; for he was so proud and ferocious, that he never would have allowed himself to seem his brother’s inferior. But Moses, without regard to Esau’s design, commends the secret providence of God, by which he was driven into exile, that the possession of the land might remain free for Jacob alone. Esau removed to Mount Seir, through the desire of present advantage, as is elsewhere stated. Nothing was less in his mind than to provide for his brother’s welfare; but God directed the blind man by his own hand, that he might not occupy that place in the land which he had appointed for his own servant. Thus it often happens that the wicked do good to the elect children of God, contrary to their own intention; and while their hasty cupidity pants for present advantages, they promote the eternal salvation of those whose destruction they have sometimes desired. Let us, then, learn from the passage before us, to see, by the eyes of faith, both in accidental circumstances (as they are called) and in the evil desires of men, that secret providence of God, which directs all events to a result predetermined by himself. For when Esau went forth, that he might live more commodiously apart from his father’s family, he is said to have departed from the face of his brother, because the Lord had so determined it. It is stated indefinitely, that he departed “into the country;” because, being in uncertainty respecting his plan, he sought a home in various places, until Mount Seir presented itself; and as we say, he went out at a venture. <note n="129"> <div sID="gen4655" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="la">Quemadmodum Gallice dicitur</foreign>, <foreign xml:lang="fr">Il s’en est alle a son aventure</foreign>.<div eID="gen4655" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen4654" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.36.6" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen4653" osisID="Gen.36.6" type="section"/>
entries.e5f2bbb7e471016e712db3171941dfea9741e2f8: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.36.9" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.36.9" sID="gen4656" type="section"/> <div sID="gen4657" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">9.</hi> <hi type="italic">And these are the generations of Esau, the father of the Edomites</hi> <note n="130"> <div sID="gen4658" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="la">Patris Edom</foreign>.<div eID="gen4658" type="x-p"/> </note> Though Esau had two names, yet in this place the second name refers to his posterity, who are called Idumeans. For, to make it appear what God had bestowed upon him for the sake of his father Isaac, Moses expressly calls him the father of a celebrated and famous people. And certainly, it served this purpose not a little, to trace the effect and fulfillment of the prophecy in the progeny of Esau.
